nodes.description: IMPDH1 assembles into octamers and micron-scale filaments (cytoophidia) whose architecture tunes activity. Disease variants form abnormally large, persistent and mislocalized filaments rather than dynamic ones; in zebrafish cones the mutant filaments sit at synapses and, for D226N, inside nuclei. In cultured cells D226N produces cytoophidia in most cells and is not dispersed by guanosine. Whether the abnormal filament is itself toxic or a marker of deregulation is not settled.

nodes.description: A partly independent branch: the mutant protein misfolds, and in refolding experiments with equimolar mixtures of normal and mutant enzyme the activity regained is close to the pure-mutant figure, indicating that in hybrid tetramers mutant subunits impose their faulty conformation on wild-type partners. This molecular recruitment offers a basis for the dominant inheritance. The claim is contested against the finding that the same variants have no effect on protein stability or aggregation, so it is curated as one competing mechanism rather than a settled one.

nodes.description: A heterozygous missense (occasionally in-frame) variant arises in IMPDH1, clustered in and immediately downstream of the regulatory CBS (Bateman) domain encoded by exons 8-10, where the recurrent p.Asp226Asn allele lies. The variant is the initiating lesion. Critically, it does not reduce catalytic activity and does not perturb the bulk guanine nucleotide pool; its consequences are on allosteric regulation, higher-order assembly and a moonlighting nucleic-acid-binding function, with a dominant-negative component. Truncating variants and missense variants outside exons 8-10 are mostly not disease-causing, and gnomAD shows IMPDH1 loss of function is tolerated, so PVS1 does not apply to this gene for this disease.

genetic_context.description: Heterozygous germline missense variant in or downstream of the CBS domain (exons 8-10). Catalytic activity is preserved; the pathogenic consequence is loss of allosteric regulation and of nucleic-acid binding, with evidence that mutant subunits impose their conformation on wild-type subunits in hybrid tetramers.

nodes.description: Independent of catalysis, IMPDH1 binds single-stranded nucleic acids and associates with polyribosomes, including those translating rhodopsin mRNA, through the subdomain that harbours the disease mutations. Disease variants reduce the affinity and specificity of this binding and the most common allele, D226N, disrupts polyribosome association of a retinal isoform. Because perturbed rhodopsin expression can trigger photoreceptor apoptosis, loss of this moonlighting function is a candidate route to degeneration, though the pathogenic consequence is inferred rather than demonstrated.

nodes.description: A germline null. It shows only slowly progressive retinal degeneration with most photoreceptors structurally intact at 12 months, in contrast to the severe human dominant disease. Its mildness is the contrast the field used to argue against a loss-of-catalysis mechanism, and it models autosomal recessive, not dominant, disease.

evidence.snippet: Impdh1(-/-) null mice are shown here to display a slowly progressive form of retinal degeneration in which visual transduction, analysed by electroretinographic wave functions, becomes gradually compromised, although at 12 months of age most photoreceptors remain structurally intact.

nodes.description: Disease variants in the CBS (Bateman) domain disrupt allosteric control of the enzyme by purine nucleotides. The p.Asp226Asn allele confers resistance to feedback inhibition by GDP/GTP, and p.Arg224Pro abolishes ATP binding at the regulatory site. Cryo-EM shows the disease mutations split into two functional classes, one that disrupts GTP regulation and one that does not, so loss of regulation is variant-specific rather than universal.

nodes.description: The convergent outcome is progressive photoreceptor dysfunction and death, rods before cones and periphery before centre. Dark-adapted rod electroretinogram responses are extinguished before light-adapted cone responses, rod loss exceeds cone loss at all ages, and the peripheral retina is more susceptible than the centre, so central function is relatively preserved until late. The final step from molecular defect to photoreceptor death is not fully established and may be the sum of the filament, nucleic-acid-binding and misfolding branches.

nodes.description: Although IMPDH1 is ubiquitously expressed, the retina uniquely depends on it: IMPDH1 is higher in retina than any other tissue, is concentrated in photoreceptor inner segments and synaptic terminals, and is expressed there as retina-exclusive splice and translation-start isoforms (IMPDH1(546), IMPDH1(595)) that encode distinct proteins with altered regulation. In mouse retina IMPDH1 generates the bulk of photoreceptor GTP, so a housekeeping enzyme is non-redundant in this one tissue. This dependence is why CBS-domain variants damage photoreceptors specifically.

evidence.snippet: IMPDH1 is found predominately in the inner segment and synaptic terminals of retinal photoreceptors. The predominant transcripts of IMPDH1 in human retina are the result of alternate splicing and alternate start sites of translation.
